tagline: A stage road across an older desert trading route.
intro: The Bradshaw Trail crosses the Colorado Desert on seventy miles of graded dirt, with the Orocopia Mountains near the western start and the Mule Mountains toward the eastern end. Soft sand interrupts the going. Long before the stagecoaches, this was an Indigenous trade route.

In 1862 a Cahuilla chief, Cabazon, and a visiting Maricopa told William Bradshaw where the springs and water holes lay. He made a stage road of it, and until 1877 it carried miners and other passengers toward the gold fields at La Paz.

moments.title: Orocopia Mountains
moments.text: Near the western start the road keeps company with the Orocopia Mountains, through whose southeastern foothills the old trail passed.

moments.title: Chuckwalla Mountains
moments.text: The Chuckwalla Mountains run along the north side of the road. Bradshaw's party skirted their southern end, and Chuckwalla Springs was one of its water holes.

moments.title: Mule Mountains
moments.text: The Mule Mountains rise toward the eastern end, where Bradshaw's party crossed through a gap to reach the Palo Verde Valley.

practical: Four-wheel drive is recommended for the stretches of soft sand, and there are no amenities on the trail itself. The Chocolate Mountain Aerial Gunnery Range, a posted live bombing range, borders part of the road to the south.

sources.label: BLM, Bradshaw Trail Back Country Byway
